'''Carl Nelson Gorman''' (October 5, 1907 – January 29, 1998), also known as '''Kin-Ya-Onny-Beyeh''', was a Navajo [[code talker]], visual artist, painter, illustrator, and professor. He was on the faculty at the [[University of California, Davis]], from 1950 until 1973. During [[World War II]], Gorman served as a code talker with the [[United States Marine Corps]] in the [[Pacific War|Pacific]].<ref name=":03">{{Cite news|last=Thomas |first=Robert Jr.|date=1998-02-01|title=Carl Gorman, Code Talker In World War II, Dies at 90|language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/02/01/us/carl-gorman-code-talker-in-world-war-ii-dies-at-90.html|access-date=2021-09-15|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref name=":13">{{Cite news|date=1998-01-31|title=Artist Carl Gorman Dies At 90|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/local/1998/01/31/artist-carl-gorman-dies-at-90/061476ee-0b89-4f55-bebc-3d453a0cc8cb/ |access-date=2021-09-15|newspaper=Washington Post}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
[[File:Carl Gorman and 1907 house.jpg|thumb|Gorman (1985) stands outside the house in which he was born in 1907 in [[Chinle, Arizona]]|left]]
Carl Nelson Gorman was born on October 5, 1907, in [[Chinle, Arizona]].<ref name=":03"/> Chinle is located on the rim of the [[Canyon de Chelly National Monument]]. He was a member of the ''Dibeh Łizhin'' clan (the Black Sheep Clan) and born for the ''Khinyá' áni'' clan (the Towering House People).<ref>{{Cite book|last=Monthan|first=Doris Born|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=uRI4AQAAIAAJ|title=R. C. Gorman: The Lithographs|publisher=Northland Press|year=1978|isbn=9780873581790|location=Santa Fe, NM|pages=5}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last1=Greenberg |first1=Henry |last2=Greenberg |first2=Georgia |title=Carl Gorman's World |publisher= Univ of New Mexico Press |year=1984 |isbn=978-0826307385}}</ref> His father was a cattleman and "[[Native American trade|Indian trader]]".<ref name=":52">{{Cite book |last=Griffin-Pierce |first=Trudy |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Ih-tAgAAQBAJ |title=The Columbia Guide to American Indians of the Southwest |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-231-12790-5 |series=Columbia Guides to American Indian History and Culture |language=en |author-link=Trudy Griffin-Pierce}}</ref> When he was a child, his mother Alice, who was a traditional weaver,  supported his earliest artistic pursuits.<ref name=":34">{{Cite book|last=Rosebrough|first=Elizabeth Hardin-Burrola, Carol Sarath, and Bob|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9esmDwAAQBAJ|title=Legendary Locals of Gallup|date=2017|publisher=Arcadia Publishing|isbn=978-1-4671-2567-3|pages=109|language=en}}</ref><ref name=":52"/> His mother also worked to translate hymns from English into Navajo.<ref name=":52"/> His parents gave a portion of their land to found the First Presbyterian Mission in Chinle.<ref name=":52"/><ref name=":0" />
Gorman's western education began at the Rehoboth Mission School in [[Rehoboth, New Mexico]]; an [[American Indian boarding schools|American Indian boarding school]] where he was punished for speaking the Navajo language.<ref name=":24">{{Cite web|last=Holder|first=Kathleen|date=May 19, 2009|title=Looking Back, Namesakes: Carl N. Gorman|url=https://centennial.ucdavis.edu/timeline/history/namesakes/gorman.html|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-15|website=UC Davis Centennial|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090723085304/http://centennial.ucdavis.edu/timeline/history/namesakes/gorman.html|archive-date=2009-07-23}}</ref><ref name=":42">{{Cite book|last1=Melton|first1=Brad|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r-yz5_3Jf1gC|title=Arizona Goes to War: The Home Front and the Front Lines During World War II|last2=Smith|first2=Dean|date= 2003|publisher=University of Arizona Press|isbn=978-0-8165-2190-6|language=en}}</ref> His father removed him from the school and enrolled him in the [[Albuquerque Indian School]] in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico]]<ref name=":0" /> where he excelled at sports including boxing and football.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gorman |first=Michael |date=July 7, 2022 |title=Dr. Carl N. Gorman |url=https://www.michaelgormangallery.com/carl-n-gorman |website=Michael Gorman Gallery}}</ref>

== Career ==
In April 1942, Gorman was one of 29 Navajo men recruited by the United States Marine Corps to create a code based on the [[Navajo language]].<ref name=":13"/><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":42" /> The Navajo code talkers fought and deployed the code in every campaign from [[Guadalcanal campaign|Guadalcanal]] through the [[Occupation of Japan]]. Gorman served in four campaigns: Guadalcanal, [[Battle of Saipan|Saipan]], [[Battle of Tinian|Tinian]], and [[Battle of Tarawa|Tarawa]].<ref name=":0" /> The Navajo code was formally developed and modeled on the [[Allied military phonetic spelling alphabets|Joint Army/Navy Phonetic Alphabet]] that uses agreed-upon English words to represent letters or other meanings.<ref name=":13" /> The Japanese were never able to crack the Navajo-based encryption.<ref name=":24" /> In 1945, Gorman was honorably discharged as [[Private first class|Private First Class]].<ref name=":0" />

After the war, Gorman studied art at the Otis Art Institute (now [[Otis College of Art and Design]]), on the [[G.I. Bill]].<ref name=":34"/><ref name=":52"/> In 1949, Gorman was working as an illustrator in Los Angeles,<ref name=":24"/> including [[technical illustration]] work for [[Douglas Aircraft Company]].

In 1950, he joined the faculty at UC Davis, where he remained until 1973.<ref name=":24"/> Gorman helped in the formation of the Native American Studies Department, as well as in the creation of a Native American art studio workshop.<ref name=":24"/> In 1969, the Native American Studies Department at UC Davis was formed under the name ''Tehcumseh Center'', Gorman was one of the first faculty working alongside [[Jack D. Forbes]], and [[David Risling]], Jr.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Lutz|first=Hartmut|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cA4WAQAAIAAJ|title=D-Q University: Native American Self-determination in Higher Education|date=1980|publisher=Department of Applied Behavioral Sciences, Native American Studies, Tecumseh Center|pages=22|language=en}}</ref> {{Interlanguage link|Sarah V. Hutchison|qid=Q108556934}} joined the faculty in 1970,<ref name=":2" /> and [[George Longfish]] joined in 1973.

Gorman used traditional Navajo motifs in his visual art practice.<ref name=":52" />

Around 1973, Gorman and his wife Mary moved to Gallup, New Mexico where he worked on many community-based projects; including directing the Navajo Arts and Crafts Guild, he founded the Navajo Code Talkers Association, worked on an oral history project with Navajo elders, and taught classes at both Navajo Community College (now [[Diné College]]) and University of New Mexico-Gallup.<ref name=":34"/>

=== Significant dates in art career ===
[[File:Navajo Code Talker at NAU.jpg|alt=Navajo Code Talker is a Bronze bust sculpture created by famed Navajo Artist R.C. Gorman. Gorman used his father, Carl's likeness for this sculpture. Carl was a Navajo Code Talker in WWII. The face is that of an elderly Navajo man looking up and our in a proud manner. It sits on an 8ft marble base on the NAU campus in Flagstaff Arizona. Bright blue skies surround the bust with the mountains visible in the distance.|thumb|Navajo Code Talker, by R.C. Gorman at the Northern Arizona University Campus in Flagstaff, AZ. Based a small edition sculpture created by Gorman in 1978 and enlarged for the NAU campus in 1995.]]
* 1964 - Carl and his son [[R. C. Gorman|R.C. Gorman]] are invited to do a two-person show, ''"New Directions in American Indian Art"'', at the Philbrook Art Center in Tulsa, OK.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Adams (1), Newlin (2) |first=Ben (1), Richard (2) |title=R.C. Gorman - The Graphic Works |publisher=Taos Editions, Ltd. |year=1987 |isbn=0-9619950-0-9 |edition=1st |location=Albuquerque, NM |pages=232–238}}</ref>
* 1965 - Carl and R.C. exhibit together at the [[Heard Museum]]'s Gallery of Indian Art in Phoenix, Arizona. John Becklaw, rights a review in the Arizona Republic under the headline: "Gormans-Father and Son Rebels in Indian Art"<ref name=":02" />
* 1968 - Carl loans his son, R.C. Gorman some money to purchase the Manchester Gallery in Taos, NM. R.C. renames it the Navajo Gallery.<ref name=":02" /> It is the first Native American owned fine art gallery.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Gorman |first=Michael |date=July 10, 2022 |title=Home |url=http://www.MichaelGormanGallery.com |access-date=July 10, 2022}}</ref>
* 1990 - Gorman was awarded a [[Doctor of Humane Letters|doctor of humane letters]] from [[University of New Mexico]].
* 2020 - Carl's work is featured in the ''Smithsonian Magazine's'' November issue under the heading "''The Remarkable and Complex Legacy of Native American Military Service''".

=== Significant dates in military career ===

* 1941 - May 4. Carl and 28 other Navajos are sworn into the Marine Corps. They are transported by bus to [[Marine Corps Recruit Depot San Diego|MCRD San Diego]] and designated Platoon 382 - the first "''all Indian, all Navajo''" Platoon in Marine Corps history.<ref name=":1" />
* 1944 - PFC Gorman is photographed while serving on Saipan. He and a fellow code talker are injured while on litter duty when a mortar shell explodes near them.
* 1945 - PFC Gorman is Honorably discharged from the Marine Corps out of a Marine base in Oregon. Awards and Decorations include: [[Marine Corps Good Conduct Medal|Marine Good Conduct Medal]], [[American Campaign Medal]], [[Asiatic–Pacific Campaign Medal]], [[World War II Victory Medal]], [[Marksmanship badges (United States)|Marksman Badge]] with Sharpshooter tab
* 1968 - The Navajo Code is declassified.
* 1973 - Carl Gorman is elected president of the Navajo Code Talkers' Association
* 2000 - [[Jeff Bingaman|Senator Jeff Bingaman]] sponsors the Honoring Navajo Code Talkers Act
* 2001 - Carl's widow, Mary E. Gorman (Wilson) accepts a Congressional Medal from Pres. George W. Bush on behalf of Carl.

== Death, honors, and legacy ==
Gorman died from cancer on January 29, 1998, in [[Gallup, New Mexico]].<ref name=":13"/> His son [[R. C. Gorman|R.C. Gorman]] (1931–2005) was a renowned Navajo artist.<ref name=":34"/> His daughter Zonnie Gorman is a noted historian of Navajo Code Talkers.<ref>{{Cite web|title='Growing Up With Heroes: The First Twenty-Nine Navajo Code Talkers of World War II'|url=http://news.unm.edu/news/the-first-twenty-nine-navajo-code-talkers|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-15|website=UNM Newsroom|publisher=[[University of New Mexico]]|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161028083848/http://news.unm.edu/news/the-first-twenty-nine-navajo-code-talkers|archive-date=2016-10-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Navajo Code Talkers: Zonnie Gorman|url=https://www.history.com/topics/native-american-history/navajo-code-talkers-zonnie-gorman-video|url-status=live|website=The History Channel|publisher=A&E Television Networks, LLC|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112000433/https://www.history.com/topics/native-american-history/navajo-code-talkers-zonnie-gorman-video |archive-date=2020-11-12 }}</ref> His son Alfred Kee Gorman (1957–1966) also was an artist, but he died at an early age.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2013-06-25|title=Exhibitions: C.N. Gorman Museum's Navajo Summer|url=https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/exhibitions-cn-gorman-museums-navajo-summer|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-17|website=UC Davis|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210718164924/https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/exhibitions-cn-gorman-museums-navajo-summer |archive-date=2021-07-18 }}</ref>

In 1990, Gorman was awarded a [[Doctor of Humane Letters|doctor of humane letters]] from the [[University of New Mexico]].<ref name=":34" />

Shortly after his retirement in 1973, UC Davis named their new museum, the ''C.N. Gorman Museum'' in his honor, and Gorman donated to the collection.<ref name=":24"/><ref name=":34" /> In 1995, [[Northern Arizona University]] unveiled a code talker monument, a bust of Gorman sculpted by his son, R.C. Gorman.<ref name=":24" />

===Museum collections and exhibitions===
His artwork is included in the permanent museum collections of the [[C.N. Gorman Museum]],<ref name="CNGORMANMUS">{{cite web |title=Carl Nelson Gorman, Chumash Rock Painting I |url=https://gormanmuseum.ucdavis.edu/collection-piece/carl-nelson-gorman-chumash-rock-painting-i |website=gormanmuseum.ucdavis.edu |date=17 August 2021 }}</ref> the [[Brooklyn Museum]],<ref name="BAM">{{cite web|title=Brooklyn Museum|url=https://www.brooklynmuseum.org/opencollection/search?keyword=Carl+Nelson+Gorman|website=www.brooklynmuseum.org}}</ref> and the [[National Museum of the American Indian]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Deer Herder|url=https://americanindian.si.edu/collections-search/objects/NMAI_278550?destination=edan_searchtab%3Fedan_q%3D%252A%253A%252A&edan_fq%255B0%255D=set_name%253A%2522Din%25C3%25A9%2520%2528Navajo%2529%2522&edan_fq%255B1%255D=place%253A%2522Chinle%252C%2520Navajo%2520Reservation%2522|url-status=live|access-date=2021-09-15|website=National Museum of the American Indian, Smithsonian|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210911231359/https://americanindian.si.edu/collections-search/objects/NMAI_278550?destination=edan_searchtab%3Fedan_q%3D%252A%253A%252A%26edan_fq%255B0%255D%3Dset_name%253A%2522Din%25C3%25A9%2520%2528Navajo%2529%2522%26edan_fq%255B1%255D%3Dplace%253A%2522Chinle%252C%2520Navajo%2520Reservation%2522|archive-date=2021-09-11}}</ref>

In addition to the many public and private collections of Gorman's work, the Gorman Family has an extensive collection of his artworks, notes, and other ephemera. The Michael Gorman Gallery in [[Taos, New Mexico]], regularly includes rare artwork by the late Carl N. Gorman.
